docs.title: filevet
docs.text:
filevet is a self-hosted scanner for the files finance teams receive: invoices, bank statements, KYC documents and payment files. It checks them for security risks before anyone opens them or feeds them to another system.

Several independent analyzers read each file. They look for active content and known malware, attacks on the parsers that will read the file, signs that a document was edited after it was issued, financial data that doesn't add up, and text hidden from people but read by an LLM. Their findings go into one JSON report, and a policy turns them into a verdict: block, review, pass_with_findings or pass.

filevet runs as a CLI, a Python library, a REST API with async workers, or a Helm release on Kubernetes. It never runs, renders or uploads the files it scans, and each analyzer works in its own sandboxed worker.

pipx install filevet
filevet scan statement.pdf

docs.text:

  • Policies and the policy cookbook show how to tune verdicts.

  • API stability lists what 1.x promises not to break.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Fintechs and finance teams receive files from outside all the time: invoices, bank statements, KYC documents, payment files. A file can carry malware, exploit the parser that reads it, be altered to commit fraud, or hide instructions aimed at AI systems that process it. Commercial tools exist but are closed and expensive. Open-source tools cover parts of the problem, and none of them understand financial file formats.

docs.title: What filevet is
docs.text: A self-hosted, open-source tool that inspects a file with several independent analyzers and returns one report: what was checked, what was found, how severe it is, and a recommended verdict of block, review, or pass with findings.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text: Engineering and security teams at fintechs, payment companies and finance departments. They run it in upload pipelines, back-office tooling, CI, or AI ingestion pipelines.

docs.title: What it promises
docs.text:
• Every finding has a rule ID, a location, evidence and an explanation.
  • It runs entirely on your infrastructure. Files never leave it, and by default nothing is kept after the scan.
  • Verdicts come from a configurable policy, not hard-coded logic.

docs.title: What it does not promise
docs.text:
• It never declares a file safe. It reports what it checked and what it found. No scanner catches everything.
  • It does not replace antivirus or EDR, email security, or human review of high-value payments.
  • It never executes or opens files outside its sandbox.

docs.title: File types in v0.1
docs.text: PDF, CSV, XLSX, ISO 20022 XML (camt.05x, pain.001, pain.008), and ZIP archives containing these.

docs.title: Threat model for v0.1
docs.text:
1. Embedded malware and active content: macros, PDF JavaScript, launch actions, embedded executables.
  2. Parser attacks: CSV formula injection, XXE and entity expansion, zip bombs, path traversal in archives.
  3. Disguised files: extension and content mismatch, polyglots.

docs.title: Planned for later
docs.text:
• v0.2: document tampering and financial data integrity.
  • v0.3: hidden content aimed at AI or LLM pipelines.
  • v1.0: a stronger sandbox, fuzzing, a Helm chart, sanitized output for PDF, CSV and XLSX, and a stable API.

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text: Network traffic analysis, endpoint protection, malware family attribution, and storing or sharing scanned files.

docs.title: Design principles
docs.text:
• Self-hosted first.
  • No file retention.
  • Findings are explainable.
  • Findings are kept separate from policy.
  • Analyzers are plugins.
  • Every parser runs in isolation.
  • No real malware in the repository.

docs.title: v0.1 success criteria
docs.text:
• filevet scan <file> and docker run both work.
  • It flags every sample in the synthetic malicious corpus and gives no block verdicts on the synthetic benign corpus.
  • Results are available as JSON.
  • Installing from the README takes under five minutes.

docs.title: REST API
docs.text:
filevet serve runs an HTTP API. Install it with the server extra:

pip install 'filevet[server]'
export FILEVET_API_KEYS="$(printf %s "$MY_KEY" | sha256sum | cut -d' ' -f1)"
filevet serve --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000

The OpenAPI spec is in openapi.json and at /openapi.json on a running server.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
Method and path Auth Does POST /v1/scans yes Scans an upload, sent as a raw body or as a multipart/form-data field named file. ?name= sets the file name for a raw body, and ?callback= asks for a webhook GET /v1/scans/{id} yes Status (queued, done or error) and the report of an async scan GET /v1/analyzers yes Registered analyzers and the types they support GET /v1/policies yes The active policy and the built-in ones GET /healthz no The process is up GET /readyz no The queue answers, and so does ClamAV when FILEVET_CLAMD is set. 503 if not GET /metrics no Prometheus metrics

Uploads up to FILEVET_SYNC_MAX_BYTES are scanned straight away and answered with 200 and the report. The API runs at most one synchronous scan per CPU and answers 503 when all of them are busy. Larger uploads get 202, a scan ID and a Location header. A worker scans them, and GET /v1/scans/{id} returns the report until it expires.

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $MY_KEY" --data-binary @invoice.pdf \
  "http://localhost:8000/v1/scans?name=invoice.pdf"

docs.title: Async mode
docs.text:
docker compose up -d api worker redis clamav

The API puts each large upload in Redis, encrypted with Fernet under FILEVET_SPOOL_KEY, and pushes its ID onto a queue. A filevet worker takes the ID, deletes the upload from Redis as it reads it, scans it in its own temp directory, and stores the report for FILEVET_RETENTION_S seconds. The API never parses an async upload. Run as many workers as you need.

Without FILEVET_REDIS_URL the API keeps the queue in memory and runs one worker thread in its own process. That's meant for development.

The queue is the Backend protocol in filevet/interfaces/jobs.py. Another backend, such as Kafka or SQS, implements the same methods.

docs.title: Webhooks
docs.text: With ?callback=https://…, the worker POSTs the finished result to that URL. The body is signed with HMAC-SHA256 and the signature is sent as X-Filevet-Signature: sha256=<hex>. Check it with FILEVET_WEBHOOK_SECRET before trusting the body. Only https URLs on hosts listed in FILEVET_WEBHOOK_HOSTS are accepted, and redirects aren't followed, so the API can't be used to make requests to arbitrary hosts. In the Compose file the worker sits on an internal network with no route out, so webhooks need a network with egress added to the worker service.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Metric Labels filevet_scans_total verdict filevet_analyzer_runs_total analyzer, status (ok, error, timeout) filevet_analyzer_duration_seconds (summary, _sum and _count) analyzer

With Redis, the counters live in Redis, so every API replica reports the totals for all workers.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Variable Default Effect FILEVET_API_KEYS Comma-separated SHA-256 hashes of the API keys. Keys are sent as Authorization: Bearer <key> or X-API-Key FILEVET_API_NO_AUTH 1 turns API keys off, for use behind a proxy that does mTLS. The server won't start with neither set FILEVET_SYNC_MAX_BYTES 5 MiB Uploads up to this size are scanned synchronously FILEVET_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES 50 MiB Larger uploads get 413 FILEVET_RATE_LIMIT 60 Requests per minute per API key (per client address without keys) FILEVET_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_S 120 Every request is cut off with 504 after this FILEVET_CORS_ORIGINS Comma-separated origins. CORS is off when empty FILEVET_POLICY default Policy name or file for every scan FILEVET_REDIS_URL Redis for the async queue, for example redis://redis:6379/0 FILEVET_SPOOL_KEY Fernet key shared by the API and the workers. Required with Redis. Generate one with python -c "from cryptography.fernet import Fernet; print(Fernet.generate_key().decode())" FILEVET_RETENTION_S 3600 How long results and queued uploads are kept FILEVET_WEBHOOK_HOSTS Hosts that callbacks may go to FILEVET_WEBHOOK_SECRET HMAC key for webhook signatures. Webhooks are off without it

docs.title: Security notes
docs.text:
• API keys are stored only as SHA-256 hashes and compared in constant time.
  • Request bodies are counted as they arrive and cut off past the upload limit, with or without a Content-Length.
  • Nothing is written to disk by the API except the scan's private temp directory, which is deleted afterwards. Queued uploads stay encrypted in Redis until a worker takes them.
  • The interactive docs pages (/docs, /redoc) are off, because they load scripts from a CDN.
  • The rate limit is per process. Put a proxy in front for limits shared across replicas.
  • The Compose file publishes the API on 127.0.0.1 only, and Redis is capped at 2 GB without eviction, so a flood of queued uploads gets errors instead of pushing results out.
  • The request timeout ends the HTTP request. A synchronous scan that's already running finishes in the background, within the per-analyzer timeouts.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: This is the design as built so far. The pipeline and contracts are in src/filevet/core/, the analyzers in src/filevet/analyzers/, the verdict policies in src/filevet/policies/, and the CLI and REST API in src/filevet/interfaces/.

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    In[Untrusted file] --> Ingest
    Ingest[Ingest<br/>size limit, private temp copy, hashes] --> Identify
    Identify[Identify<br/>type from magic bytes] --> Dispatch
    Dispatch[Dispatch<br/>every analyzer whose supports is true] --> W1[Analyzer worker]
    Dispatch --> W2[Analyzer worker]
    Dispatch --> W3[Analyzer worker]
    W1 & W2 & W3 -- findings --> Aggregate
    W1 & W2 & W3 -- extracted children --> Recurse
    Recurse[Recurse<br/>depth, count and size limits] --> Identify
    Aggregate[Aggregate<br/>findings] --> Policy[Policy<br/>overrides, suppressions, verdict] --> Report[Report JSON]
    Aggregate --> Cleanup[Cleanup<br/>delete temp files]
  1. Ingest rejects files over the size limit (50 MB by default) with a usage error, copies the input into a private temp directory, and computes its SHA-256 and MD5. Each copy is created 0600 and made read-only (0400) before any analyzer sees it.
  2. Identify detects the type from magic bytes with the built-in signature table in core/identify.py (see ADR 9), and takes the declared type from the extension. If the two contradict each other, basic.type_mismatch reports it.
  3. Dispatch runs every analyzer that supports the artifact, each in its own worker.
  4. Recurse feeds extracted children (archive entries, PDF attachments, embedded OLE objects) back into Identify, within max_depth, max_children and max_total_expanded_bytes.
  5. Aggregate collects artifacts, findings and analyzer runs. When a recursion limit is hit, the rest of the extracted content is skipped and the pipeline adds one pipeline.limit_exceeded finding (severity high) per limit.
  6. Policy builds the report from them: it applies severity overrides, moves suppressed findings aside, and sets the verdict (block, review, pass_with_findings or pass) together with the rule that decided it. See policies.md.
  7. Cleanup always deletes temp files, including after errors.

docs.title: Core contracts
docs.text:
There are three contracts. Analyzers depend only on these, never on each other.

Artifact: one file being scanned, either the input or an extracted child. It's immutable and holds an ID, name, size, hashes, declared and detected types, depth, parent ID and a path to a read-only copy. The pipeline owns the file; analyzers only read it.

Analyzer: a protocol. analyze returns an AnalyzerResult with findings and extracted children. The AnalysisContext it receives holds the limits, the expected values from the --context file (Expected), and whether to mask IBANs in evidence.

class Analyzer(Protocol):
    name: str
    version: str

    def supports(self, artifact: Artifact) -> bool: ...
    def analyze(self, artifact: Artifact, ctx: AnalysisContext) -> AnalyzerResult: ...

Finding: one observation. It has a stable namespaced rule_id (parser.csv_formula_injection), title, description, severity (info to critical), confidence, artifact ID, location (page, cell, XPath, byte offset or archive path), evidence of at most 256 escaped characters, references (CVE, CWE, OWASP) and the analyzer that produced it.

The pipeline stamps each finding with the artifact ID and the analyzer's name and version, so an analyzer only fills in what it observed.

Findings say what was seen. The policy decides what to do about it (block, review or pass with findings), so changing the policy never means changing an analyzer.

The JSON schema of the report, which includes Finding and Artifact, is a public contract. It's committed at schema/report.schema.json and printed by filevet schema. A test fails if the two drift apart. All three models are pydantic models (ADR 7).

docs.title: Isolation model
docs.text:
Every analyzer run goes through a Sandbox (core/sandbox.py), chosen with FILEVET_SANDBOX or the sandbox= argument. The process handles one artifact and is then killed, so no state leaks between files. Each run has a wall-clock timeout (30 s by default) and a memory cap (1 GB by default, via RLIMIT_AS). The result comes back as JSON, which the pipeline validates against AnalyzerResult before using it. Nothing crosses the boundary as a pickle. If an analyzer times out, crashes, raises, returns something invalid or sends a result that's too large, the scan records a pipeline.analyzer_error finding with severity high and goes on with the other analyzers. Only the exception type goes into the report, never its message, because a message can quote file contents.

The subprocess backend forks the worker (ADR 6). The nsjail and gvisor backends start a fresh interpreter in a jail with no network, a read-only root holding only the Python runtime, the sample and a small tmpfs, a non-root user with no capabilities, no_new_privs, a seccomp allow-list and limits on CPU, memory, files and processes (ADR 13). What each backend guarantees, and where it stops, is in security-model.md.

Logs hold hashes, rule IDs and timings only, never file contents.

docs.title: Built-in analyzers
docs.text:
Analyzers are grouped in families that match their rule ID prefix: basic, malware, parser, format, integrity and ai. The integrity and AI analyzers share a raw PDF reader (core/pdf.py). The integrity analyzers also use the financial entity extractor in core/extract_finance.py, and are described in integrity.md.

ai.hidden_content reads text through core/extract_text.py, which turns a PDF, OOXML file or text file into runs of text, each marked as body, metadata or comment and with the reason it's hidden, if it is. The PDF reader records each text run's rendering mode, fill colour and opacity, and where images are drawn, so the extractor can tell invisible, white, tiny, off-page and covered text apart from an OCR layer over a scan. filevet extract runs the same extractor in an isolated worker and prints only the visible runs with --visible-only. Some of them also act as format handlers and return children for the pipeline to scan:

Analyzer Extracts parser.archive ZIP entries, including the parts of OOXML files, within the ratio, size and count limits malware.pdf_active_content PDF embedded files malware.office_macros OLE Ole10Native packages parser.polyglot The second file hidden inside a polyglot

So a macro in an .xlsm is found in two steps: parser.archive extracts xl/vbaProject.bin, and malware.office_macros reads its VBA when that child comes back through the pipeline. Analyzers read their input with Artifact.read(limit), so every read is bounded. Libraries and the reasons for them are in ADR 10.

Three environment variables configure them:

Variable Effect FILEVET_CLAMD Address of clamd, unix:/path/clamd.sock or tcp:host:port. Without it malware.clamav doesn't run FILEVET_YARA_RULES Extra directories of .yar files, separated by :, loaded next to the bundled rules FILEVET_XSD_DIR Directory of ISO 20022 XSDs named <message>.xsd, for example camt.053.001.08.xsd

docs.title: Plugin model
docs.text:
Analyzers are found through the filevet.analyzers entry point group. CONTRIBUTING.md shows how to register one.

Built-in analyzers register the same way as third-party ones, so a separate package can add analyzers without forking filevet (ADR 8). filevet analyzers lists everything registered and the detected types each one supports. It works that out by calling supports() once per known type. The test suite includes a separate example plugin package in tests/plugin/.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text: The reasons behind these choices are recorded in adr/.

docs.title: Interfaces
docs.text:
• CLI (interfaces/cli.py): scan, extract, sanitize, policy test, serve, worker and the informational commands. sanitize (filevet/sanitize.py) runs in the same sandbox as the analyzers (sanitize.md). Output formats (SARIF, JUnit XML, Markdown) are in interfaces/formats.py.
  • Library: filevet.scan, filevet.ascan, filevet.extract_text, filevet.sanitize and filevet.Policy. What's public from 1.0 is listed in stability.md. ascan runs the scan in a thread, so the event loop isn't blocked.
  • REST API (interfaces/api.py, FastAPI): small uploads are scanned in the request, larger ones are queued. The queue (interfaces/jobs.py) is a small Backend protocol with a Redis implementation for production and an in-memory one for development (ADR 12). Queued uploads are encrypted with Fernet. Workers run the same pipeline, so the isolation model is the same for every interface. Details are in api.md, and the Helm chart is described in kubernetes.md.
  • LLM second opinion (filevet/llm.py): an optional verifier found through the filevet.llm_verifiers entry point group. It sees one ai.* finding at a time, can only raise its confidence, and is never called unless --llm-verify names it.

docs.title: Capacity planning
docs.text:
These numbers come from one laptop CPU (Intel Core i5-5350U, 2 cores at 1.8 GHz) running the subprocess sandbox, Python 3.12 and every built-in analyzer except ClamAV. A current server core is roughly twice as fast. Treat them as a starting point and run the benchmarks on your own hardware:

uv run pytest benchmarks

docs.title: Time per file
docs.text:
Analyzers run one after another for each artifact, so the time for a file is the sum of its analyzer runs. One worker process handles one file at a time.

File Size Scan time Slowest analyzers PDF invoice with JavaScript 1 KB 0.5 s malware.yara, integrity.pdf_tampering, malware.pdf_active_content Bank statement CSV, 1,000 rows 84 KB 0.6 s ai.hidden_content, parser.csv_formula_injection camt.053 statement, 1,000 entries 216 KB 0.5 s ai.hidden_content, integrity.financial_data XLSX, 5,000 rows 73 KB 5.9 s ai.hidden_content (it runs on the workbook and its parts), integrity.financial_data Bank statement CSV, 50,000 rows 4.3 MB 7.1 s ai.hidden_content 3.7 s, integrity.financial_data 2.2 s

Text-heavy files cost about 1.5 s per MB, most of it the Unicode and prompt-injection checks in ai.hidden_content. XLSX costs more per byte than CSV, because the compressed sheets expand and their text is read by several analyzers. Small PDFs cost a fixed 0.5 s or so, which is mostly the per-analyzer process start.

docs.title: Sandbox overhead
docs.text:
Backend Cost per analyzer run subprocess About 20 ms (one fork) nsjail, gvisor 0.3 to 1 s (a new Python process and the analyzer's imports; integrity.pdf_signature is the slowest because pyHanko takes about a second to import)

A typical PDF goes through 9 analyzers, so a jailed scan of a small file takes 4 to 5 s instead of 0.5 s. That's fine for queue workers. For the synchronous API, keep FILEVET_SYNC_MAX_BYTES low or use the subprocess backend inside a gVisor pod.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
Each analyzer run is capped at memory_bytes (1 GiB by default). Measured peaks, including the roughly 55 MB a forked worker shares with its parent:

Analyzer 4 MB CSV 73 KB XLSX Small PDF integrity.financial_data 130 MB 78 MB 58 MB ai.hidden_content 88 MB 87 MB 58 MB parser.csv_formula_injection 82 MB 87 MB n/a malware.yara 69 MB 67 MB 67 MB

Expect about 2 to 3 times the input size on top of the base for text formats. Only one analyzer runs at a time per worker, so a worker needs its base plus the largest single run: about 200 MB for 5 MB inputs, and the full memory_bytes cap for the 50 MB default input limit at worst.

docs.title: Sizing
docs.text:
• Run one worker per core. Throughput per worker is roughly 1 / (average scan time), for example about 2 small PDFs a second, or one 4 MB CSV every 7 s on the machine above.
  • For memory, 256 MB per worker covers inputs up to a few MB. Give workers that take 50 MB inputs at least memory_bytes plus 200 MB.
  • Each scan writes its input and extracted children to a private temp directory, up to max_input_bytes plus max_total_expanded_bytes (550 MB by default). In Kubernetes this is the /tmp emptyDir, which counts against the pod's memory when it's memory-backed.
  • The API runs at most one synchronous scan per CPU at a time. Everything larger than FILEVET_SYNC_MAX_BYTES goes to the queue.

docs.title: Regressions
docs.text: The Benchmarks workflow runs benchmarks/ on every push to master and stores the results as the baseline. On a pull request it runs them again and fails when any case's fastest round is more than 20% slower than the master baseline. The fastest round is used because it's the least affected by noisy CI machines.

docs.title: Policy cookbook
docs.text:
Recipes for common needs. Each one is a complete policy file you can pass to --policy, to Policy.load() or to FILEVET_POLICY. The format is described in Policies, and filevet schema policy prints its JSON schema.

Try a policy on sample files before rolling it out:

make corpus
filevet policy test ./our-policy.yaml --corpus tmp-samples/corpus

docs.title: Start from the default
docs.text:
The built-in default policy is short. Copy it and change what you need:

policy_version: 1
name: ours
rules:
  - match: { severity: [critical, high] }
    action: block
  - match: { rule_id: format.iso20022_schema }
    action: allow
  - match: { severity: medium }
    action: review
default_action: pass_with_findings

Rules are checked in order and the first match wins, so put specific rules above general ones.

docs.title: Block a rule whatever its severity
docs.text:
Macros have no place in an invoice. Block every malware.office_macros finding, including the medium ones for macros that don't auto-run:

policy_version: 1
name: no-macros
rules:
  - match: { rule_id: malware.office_macros }
    action: block
  - match: { severity: [critical, high] }
    action: block
  - match: { severity: medium }
    action: review
default_action: pass_with_findings

docs.title: Lower the severity of plain links
docs.text:
A PDF with a /URI link is common and rarely dangerous. An override changes the severity in the report before the rules run:

policy_version: 1
name: links-are-low
overrides:
  - match: { rule_id: malware.pdf_active_content, evidence_contains: "/URI" }
    severity: low
rules:
  - match: { severity: [critical, high] }
    action: block
  - match: { severity: medium }
    action: review
default_action: pass_with_findings

docs.title: Review only when tampering signals combine
docs.text:
One integrity signal on its own is often innocent: a statement that was saved twice, or a date at the edge of a period. Send a file to review only when two or more appear together:

policy_version: 1
name: combined-integrity
rules:
  - match: { severity: [critical, high] }
    action: block
  - match: { rule_id: "integrity.*" }
    action: review
    when: { min_count: 2 }
  - match: { rule_id: "integrity.*" }
    action: pass_with_findings
  - match: { severity: medium }
    action: review
default_action: pass_with_findings

The third rule catches the single integrity findings that the second one skipped, so they don't fall through to the medium rule.

docs.title: Never pass a file that wasn't fully scanned
docs.text:
When an analyzer crashes or times out, or a recursion limit stops the scan, filevet adds pipeline.analyzer_error or pipeline.limit_exceeded. Both are high, so every policy that blocks high already blocks them. If your policy is more lenient, keep a rule for them at the top:

policy_version: 1
name: lenient
rules:
  - match: { rule_id: "pipeline.*" }
    action: block
  - match: { severity: critical }
    action: block
  - match: { severity: high }
    action: review
default_action: pass_with_findings

docs.title: Roll out in review-only mode
docs.text:
While you learn what your traffic looks like, block only critical findings and send everything else to review:

policy_version: 1
name: shadow
rules:
  - match: { severity: critical }
    action: block
  - match: { severity: [high, medium, low] }
    action: review
default_action: pass_with_findings

docs.title: Silence one rule for one known file
docs.text:
Use a suppression instead of a policy change when a single file is the problem. It names the file's SHA-256, gives a reason and expires:

suppressions:
  - rule_id: parser.csv_formula_injection
    sha256: 50d858e0985ecc7f60418aaf0cc5ab587f42c2570a884095a9e8ccacd0f6545c
    reason: Supplier export with HYPERLINK formulas, checked by the AP team
    expires: 2027-03-31

filevet scan export.csv --suppressions suppressions.yaml

docs.title: Does filevet replace an antivirus?
docs.text: No. It can use ClamAV as one of its analyzers, but most of its checks are about things an antivirus doesn't look at: active content in documents, parser attacks, tampering, inconsistent financial data and text hidden from people. Run it next to your existing controls.

docs.title: Does filevet send my files anywhere?
docs.text: No. It makes no network calls while scanning. The only outbound requests are optional webhooks from the API workers, which are off unless you configure them. The optional --llm-verify hook calls whatever verifier you install and name.

docs.title: Can a scanned file harm the machine running filevet?
docs.text: That's the main risk filevet is built around. Each analyzer runs in its own worker with a timeout and memory limit, and the nsjail and gvisor backends add no network, a read-only filesystem, a seccomp filter and dropped privileges. The security model lists the guarantees of each backend and their limits.

docs.title: A legitimate file was flagged. What do I do?
docs.text: Check the rule's page in the rule reference, which lists its known false positives. For a single known file, add a suppression with a reason and an expiry date. If a rule is wrong for your traffic in general, change its action in your policy. If you think the rule itself is wrong, open an issue with a script that builds a similar file, never the file itself.

docs.title: Does an integrity finding mean the document is forged?
docs.text: No. Integrity findings are signals for review. A PDF saved twice or an IBAN that isn't on record has innocent explanations too. Integrity checks explains each technique and its limits.

docs.title: Which file types does it read?
docs.text: PDF, CSV and text, OOXML (XLSX, XLSM, DOCX, DOCM), legacy Office (XLS, DOC), XML including ISO 20022 messages, and ZIP archives. Other types are still identified, so an executable renamed to .pdf is caught.

docs.title: How big can a file be?
docs.text: 50 MB by default, with limits on recursion depth, extracted children and total expanded size. All of them are set in Limits.

docs.title: Will an upgrade break my integration?
docs.text: Not within 1.x. The CLI, report schema, policy schema, Python API, analyzer protocol and REST API v1 follow the rules in API stability.

docs.title: Fuzzing
docs.text: filevet's format handlers are fuzzed with Atheris, a coverage-guided fuzzer for Python built on libFuzzer. The harness is fuzz/fuzz.py, and the seeds are the synthetic corpus.

docs.title: Targets
docs.text:
Target What it fuzzes pdf, ooxml, ole, csv, xml, zip Every built-in analyzer that supports the type, called in-process on the input pipeline scan() with every analyzer, checking that the report is valid against docs/schema/report.schema.json

The format targets treat any exception that escapes analyze() as a crash, because an analyzer must turn bad input into a finding. ClamAV is left out because it needs a daemon.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
Atheris publishes wheels for Python 3.11, so run it on 3.11, in its own environment so your .venv stays as it is:

make corpus
mkdir -p tmp-samples/fuzz/pdf tmp-samples/fuzz/crashes
UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=.venv-fuzz uv run --python 3.11 --with atheris==2.3.0 python -I fuzz/fuzz.py pdf \
  -max_total_time=600 -timeout=30 -rss_limit_mb=2048 \
  -artifact_prefix=tmp-samples/fuzz/crashes/ \
  tmp-samples/fuzz/pdf tmp-samples/corpus

The first directory collects new interesting inputs, and the second holds the seeds. Crashes, hangs (-timeout) and out-of-memory errors (-rss_limit_mb) are written to tmp-samples/fuzz/crashes/, which git ignores. Never commit them.

docs.title: Nightly job
docs.text: The Fuzz workflow runs every target for 10 minutes each night, keeps each target's corpus in the Actions cache so coverage keeps growing, and uploads crash files as an artifact when a target fails. Start it by hand with a different time budget from the Actions tab.

docs.title: When it finds something
docs.text:
1. Download the crash artifact and reproduce it locally inside the test sandbox.
  2. Work out the smallest input that triggers it, and add a generator option to tests/corpus/generators/ that builds it. Don't commit the crash file itself.
  3. Add a test to tests/unit/test_fuzz_regressions.py, fix the bug at its root and check that the test failed before the fix.
  4. If the crash is in a dependency (qpdf, YARA, expat, olefile), report it upstream through that project's security process, and handle the error in filevet in the meantime.

The first runs found four bugs, all fixed with regression tests: an XML declaration with an unknown encoding raised LookupError in four analyzers, a corrupt deflate stream raised zlib.error inside malware.office_macros, a bare carriage return in a CSV field raised csv.Error in integrity.financial_data, and a huge startxref offset raised OverflowError in malware.pdf_active_content.

docs.title: OSS-Fuzz
docs.text: Once the project meets OSS-Fuzz's acceptance criteria, the harness can move there. OSS-Fuzz expects one fuzz_<target>.py file per target, so fuzz/fuzz.py would be split into thin wrappers around the same code. Until then the nightly job takes its place.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: filevet needs Python 3.11 or newer on Linux or macOS. The stronger sandbox backends need Linux.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
pipx install filevet
# or
uv tool install filevet

filevet scan statement.pdf

The report goes to stdout as JSON. For a quick look at a terminal, use the table format:

filevet scan --format table invoice.pdf receipts.zip

The exit code follows the verdict, so scripts and CI jobs don't have to parse the report:

Code Meaning 0 pass or pass_with_findings 1 review 2 block 3 Usage error, such as a missing file, a file over the size limit or an invalid policy 4 Internal error in filevet

--policy strict or --policy ./our-policy.yaml picks another policy. filevet --help lists every command.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
Run the image without network access and with the file mounted read-only:

docker run --rm --network none --read-only --tmpfs /tmp \
  -v "$PWD:/in:ro" ghcr.io/pablodt00/filevet scan /in/statement.pdf

The Compose file in the repository adds ClamAV as a sidecar and shares its socket with filevet:

docker compose --profile clamav up -d clamav
docker compose run --rm filevet scan /in/statement.pdf

filevet alone needs about 200 MB of RAM. ClamAV needs 1 to 2 GB more for its signature database.

docs.title: REST API
docs.text:
Install the server extra, set an API key and start the server:

pip install 'filevet[server]'
export FILEVET_API_KEYS="$(printf %s "$MY_KEY" | sha256sum | cut -d' ' -f1)"
filevet serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $MY_KEY" --data-binary @invoice.pdf \
  "http://localhost:8000/v1/scans?name=invoice.pdf"

Small uploads are answered with the report. Larger ones are queued for a filevet worker. REST API covers the endpoints, the queue and every setting.

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text: The Helm chart runs the API, the workers, Redis and optionally ClamAV, with worker egress blocked by a NetworkPolicy. Kubernetes has the install steps and a local quickstart with kind.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
from filevet import Policy, scan

report = scan("invoice.pdf", policy=Policy.load("strict"))
print(report.verdict, report.decision.reason)

ascan does the same without blocking an event loop, and extract_text(path, visible_only=True) returns only the text a person would see.

docs.title: GitHub Action
docs.text:
The repository is a GitHub Action. It scans the documents a pull request adds or changes and uploads the findings to code scanning as SARIF.

jobs:
  filevet:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      security-events: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - uses: pablodt00/filevet@v1  # pin to a release tag or commit
        with:
          policy: strict
Input Default Effect pattern common document extensions Extended regular expression for the paths to scan policy default Built-in policy name or path to a policy file fail-on block Severity or verdict that fails the step version latest filevet version to install from PyPI

The action skips symbolic links and deleted files, and passes file names after -- so a name can't be read as an option.

docs.title: pre-commit
docs.text:
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/pablodt00/filevet
    rev: v1.0.0
    hooks:
      - id: filevet

The hook fails the commit when a staged document gets a block verdict.

docs.title: Other CI systems
docs.text:
Any CI can run the CLI. Pick the output with --format:

Format For sarif GitHub code scanning and other SARIF 2.1.0 tools. Each rule links to its page in the rule reference junit CI dashboards. One test case per file, failed on review or block markdown Pull request comments table People at a terminal 
filevet scan --format junit --output filevet.xml --fail-on review -- docs/*.pdf

--fail-on <severity|verdict> makes the exit code 1 when any file reaches that severity or verdict and 0 otherwise.

docs.title: Python applications
docs.text:
The examples/ directory in the repository has three small integrations:

Example Does fastapi_upload.py An upload endpoint that scans with ascan and refuses blocked files s3_quarantine.py An S3 event handler that moves blocked or reviewed files to a quarantine bucket rag_ingestion.py Scans with the ai-ingestion policy and indexes only the visible text

docs.title: Docker Compose
docs.text:
docker-compose.yml runs the API, a worker, Redis and ClamAV. The worker and Redis sit on an internal network with no route out.

export FILEVET_SPOOL_KEY=... FILEVET_API_KEYS=...
docker compose up -d

See REST API for the settings and Kubernetes for the Helm chart.

docs.title: Integrity checks
docs.text:
A document can be dangerous without carrying malware. Someone edits the amount on a bank statement before sending it in for a loan, or swaps the IBAN on a supplier's invoice so the payment goes to their own account. filevet's integrity rules look for the traces those edits leave behind.

Integrity findings are signals for a person to review, not proof of fraud. Most rules report medium at most. The exception is a broken PDF signature, or content added after signing, which is high because the document contradicts its own seal. Until the policy engine arrives in Phase 3, the verdict follows the highest severity, so one integrity signal on its own leads to review at most. The Phase 3 policy will raise the verdict when several signals combine, such as a changed amount plus a new producer plus fonts added in the same revision.

Three analyzers produce these findings:

Analyzer Input Rules integrity.pdf_tampering PDF pdf_incremental_updates, pdf_revision_diff, pdf_producer_mismatch, pdf_text_overlay, pdf_font_anomaly integrity.pdf_signature Signed PDF pdf_digital_signature integrity.financial_data PDF text, plain text, CSV, XLSX, ISO 20022 XML iban_invalid, bic_invalid, iban_inconsistent, iban_not_allowlisted, totals_mismatch, date_anomaly, duplicate_ids

All rule IDs start with integrity.. Each one has a page in rules/.

docs.title: Saved again after creation
docs.text:
Most PDF editors don't rewrite the file when you save. They append the changed objects, a new cross-reference section and a new %%EOF at the end. The original bytes stay in place, so every earlier revision can still be read.

filevet splits the file at each startxref … %%EOF marker and sorts the objects of every later revision into page content, pages, fonts, metadata, form fields and annotations, signatures, or other. integrity.pdf_incremental_updates reports the revision count and what changed in each. A change to page content is medium. Pages, fonts or other objects alone are low, and metadata, form fields or signatures alone are info.

docs.title: What the text said before
docs.text: integrity.pdf_revision_diff extracts the text of every revision, groups it into lines by position on the page, and diffs each revision against the one before it. A changed line that contains an amount, an IBAN or a date is medium, and any other change (a name, for example) is low. The evidence shows the old and the new line, with IBANs masked.

docs.title: Who wrote the file
docs.text:
integrity.pdf_producer_mismatch compares metadata that should agree:

  • the Producer of the first revision with that of the last (low), as when a statement from a banking system was last saved by a consumer PDF editor
  • the Producer in the XMP metadata with the one in the Info dictionary (low)
  • ModDate earlier than CreationDate (medium)
  • with a context file, a producer that isn't among the expected ones for an issuer named in the document (medium)

docs.title: White boxes and text over text
docs.text: The usual way to change a figure in a PDF without an editor that understands text is to paint a white rectangle over it and write the new value on top. integrity.pdf_text_overlay runs the page content stream, tracking the transformation matrix, the fill color, text positions and filled rectangles. It reports a white rectangle painted after text and covering most of it, and text that lands on other, different text. Glyph widths are estimated, not read from font metrics.

docs.title: Fonts
docs.text: When someone retypes a number, the editor often embeds a fresh subset of the font, so the page ends up with two copies of, say, ABCDEF+Helvetica and GHIJKL+Helvetica. integrity.pdf_font_anomaly reports digits set in the rarer copy (medium), a font used for amounts and nothing else (low), and fonts added in a later revision (low).

docs.title: Signatures
docs.text:
integrity.pdf_digital_signature verifies every signature with pyHanko (ADR 11):

Result Severity Valid, trusted, covers the whole file info Valid, but the certificate is untrusted or expired low Valid, then form fields or annotations were added low Valid, then other content was added high Invalid, or the signature can't be read high

filevet trusts no certificates by default, not even the system store, so a valid signature is low until you list your CA certificates under trust_roots in the context file. It never fetches revocation data.

docs.title: Financial data
docs.text:
core/extract_finance.py pulls IBANs, BICs, amounts and dates out of text, CSV and XLSX cells, and reads ISO 20022 messages element by element instead of as text.

  • integrity.iban_invalid: the mod-97 check fails, the length is wrong for the country, or the country has no IBAN. Unlabeled text only counts when it has a known country code and the right length, so VAT numbers and creditor references (RF…) don't trigger it.
  • integrity.bic_invalid: the BIC doesn't follow the ISO 9362 layout or its country code is unknown (low). A document with exactly one IBAN and one BIC from different countries is also reported (low).
  • integrity.iban_inconsistent: a PDF or text document gives more than one labeled IBAN, such as one in the header and another in the payment instructions. Statements, CSV exports and payment files list many counterparties, so this rule skips them.
  • integrity.totals_mismatch: invoice line items plus tax don't add up to the total; opening balance plus signed entries doesn't give the closing balance; in camt.052 and camt.053, OPBD/PRCD plus the booked Ntry amounts doesn't give CLBD; in pain.001, pain.008 and pacs.008, NbOfTxs or CtrlSum doesn't match the transactions, for the group header and for each PmtInf.
  • integrity.date_anomaly: dates that don't exist (31.02.2026); in camt messages, a booking date more than 7 days after the value date, a booking date outside the statement period or after the message was created, or a creation date in the future.
  • integrity.duplicate_ids: the same MsgId, PmtInfId, InstrId, EndToEndId, TxId, NtryRef or AcctSvcrRef more than once at the same place in a message (medium in payment files, low in statements). NOTPROVIDED is ignored.

docs.title: Context file
docs.text:
filevet scan --context context.yaml adds what you already know:

parties:
  Muster Lieferant GmbH:
    ibans: [DE17123456780000000001]
  Beispiel Bank AG:
    producers: [BankCore Statements 4.2]
trust_roots:
  - |
    -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
    ...
    -----END CERTIFICATE-----

When a document names a party, integrity.iban_not_allowlisted reports any valid IBAN next to that name that isn't on record for it, which catches invoice redirection. In a PDF or text file the whole document counts as next to the name, in CSV and XLSX it's the same row, and in ISO 20022 it's the same transaction or entry. producers feeds pdf_producer_mismatch, and trust_roots feeds pdf_digital_signature.

The context file is read once by the CLI and handed to the analyzers. It's never logged, and nothing from it goes into the report except the rule that it triggered. Error messages about the file name the problem, never its contents.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• A document recreated from scratch, with no revisions, won't trigger the revision, producer-change or added-font checks. Neither will one that was flattened or printed to a new PDF.
  • Text extraction understands simple fonts and ToUnicode maps. Text in fonts without a ToUnicode map, in scanned images or in encrypted PDFs isn't read, and encrypted PDFs skip the text-based checks altogether.
  • Only Flate-compressed streams are decoded. Other filters hide content from these checks, as they do for malware.pdf_active_content.
  • An uncompressed PDF embedded inside another one adds its own %%EOF and can be counted as a revision.
  • Overlap detection estimates glyph widths, so tightly kerned or very wide text can be missed or, rarely, misreported.
  • Invoice and statement totals are found from labels (Total, Subtotal, VAT, Opening, Closing and their German, Spanish and French counterparts) and from where the amounts sit on each line. Statements are only checked when the entries carry signs, because a separate debit column can't be told apart from a credit one in plain text.
  • CII and UBL invoices aren't checked yet, and neither are duplicate invoice numbers across rows of a CSV or XLSX.
  • Without trust roots, every signature is untrusted. Revocation isn't checked.

docs.title: Local quickstart with kind
docs.text:
kind create cluster --name filevet
docker build -t filevet:test .
kind load docker-image filevet:test --name filevet

kubectl create namespace filevet
kubectl label namespace filevet pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted

export MY_KEY=change-me
helm install fv charts/filevet -n filevet \
  --set image.repository=filevet --set image.tag=test --set image.pullPolicy=Never \
  --set apiKeys="$(printf %s "$MY_KEY" | sha256sum | cut -d' ' -f1)" \
  --set clamav.enabled=true --wait --timeout 10m

kubectl -n filevet port-forward svc/fv-filevet-api 8000:8000 &
mkdir -p tmp-samples && printf '%%PDF-1.4\n%%%%EOF\n' > tmp-samples/benign.pdf
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $MY_KEY" --data-binary @tmp-samples/benign.pdf \
  "http://localhost:8000/v1/scans?name=benign.pdf"

kind's default CNI enforces NetworkPolicy, so the egress rules below are active on a local cluster too. With k3d, the built-in network policy controller does the same: k3d cluster create filevet, then k3d image import filevet:test -c filevet in place of kind load.

Remove everything with kind delete cluster --name filevet.

docs.text:
The full list with defaults is in values.yaml. The ones you will most likely change:

Generated on install and kept across upgrades existingSecret Use your own Secret with the keys FILEVET_API_KEYS, FILEVET_SPOOL_KEY and optionally FILEVET_WEBHOOK_SECRET policy default Built-in policy name or a policy file path (FILEVET_POLICY) extraEnv [] More environment variables for the API and the worker, such as FILEVET_SYNC_MAX_BYTES or FILEVET_RATE_LIMIT (see api.md) api.replicas, worker.replicas 2 Replica counts. worker.replicas is ignored when KEDA is on api.sandbox, worker.sandbox subprocess Sandbox backend (FILEVET_SANDBOX) api.runtimeClassName, worker.runtimeClassName RuntimeClass for the pods, for example gvisor worker.keda.enabled false Create a KEDA ScaledObject that scales workers on queue length. Needs KEDA installed redis.enabled, redis.externalUrl true, In-chart Redis or an external URL clamav.enabled false Deploy ClamAV and point FILEVET_CLAMD at it webhook.secret, webhook.hosts Signed webhooks. Each host also needs an egress rule in networkPolicy.extraEgress networkPolicy.apiFrom [] NetworkPolicy peers allowed to reach the API. Empty allows any source networkPolicy.extraEgress [] Extra egress rules for the API and workers, for an external Redis or webhook hosts serviceMonitor.enabled false Create a ServiceMonitor for /metrics tmpSizeLimit 1Gi Size of the in-memory /tmp where scans keep their temp copies. It counts against the pod's memory limit

The KEDA trigger reads the Redis address without credentials. If your external Redis needs a password, add a KEDA TriggerAuthentication yourself.

docs.title: Isolation
docs.text: The API scans small uploads in the request, and workers scan the queued ones, so both handle hostile files. The chart treats them the same way.

docs.title: Pod Security
docs.text:
Every pod meets the restricted Pod Security Standard: it runs as a non-root user (10001 for filevet), drops all capabilities, can't escalate privileges, uses the runtime's default seccomp profile and has a read-only root filesystem. The only writable path is an in-memory emptyDir at /tmp with a size limit. Service account tokens aren't mounted. Label the namespace so the API server rejects anything weaker:

kubectl label namespace filevet pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted

docs.title: NetworkPolicy
docs.text: Workers accept no inbound traffic, and the API only accepts traffic on port 8000. Their egress is limited to DNS, the in-chart Redis and clamd. Anything else, the internet and the Kubernetes API included, is dropped unless you add it to networkPolicy.extraEgress. Redis accepts connections only from the API and workers and has no egress. ClamAV accepts connections from the API and workers on 3310, and can reach DNS and port 443 for signature updates (networkPolicy.clamavEgress). NetworkPolicy only works if your CNI enforces it. Most do (Calico, Cilium, kindnet, k3s), but check yours.

docs.title: RuntimeClass
docs.text:
Setting worker.runtimeClassName: gvisor (and api.runtimeClassName, if the API scans in the request) runs those pods under gVisor's user-space kernel, so a parser exploit reaches gVisor instead of the host kernel. The cluster needs gVisor installed on its nodes and a RuntimeClass:

apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: gvisor
handler: runsc

Inside a gVisor pod, keep the subprocess sandbox backend. gVisor is the outer boundary, and each analyzer still gets its own process with a timeout and a memory limit. The backends and what each one guarantees are in security-model.md.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text: Every container has requests and limits. A worker runs one analyzer process at a time, capped at 1 GB of address space by default, plus the in-memory /tmp, so the worker's default limit is 3 GiB. ClamAV needs about 2 GiB to load its signatures. Adjust the numbers once you've measured your own file mix.

docs.title: Writing an analyzer plugin
docs.text: A separate Python package can add analyzers without forking filevet. filevet finds them through the filevet.analyzers entry point group, the same way it finds its own.

docs.title: The analyzer
docs.text:
An analyzer is any class with a name, a version, a supports() method and an analyze() method:

from filevet.core.analyzer import AnalysisContext, AnalyzerResult
from filevet.core.artifact import Artifact
from filevet.core.finding import Finding, Severity


class SeenText:
    name = "example.seen_text"
    version = "0.1.0"

    def supports(self, artifact: Artifact) -> bool:
        return artifact.detected_type == "text"

    def analyze(self, artifact: Artifact, ctx: AnalysisContext) -> AnalyzerResult:
        data = artifact.read(ctx.limits.max_input_bytes)
        if b"hello" not in data:
            return AnalyzerResult()
        finding = Finding(
            rule_id="example.seen_text", title="Greeting found", severity=Severity.INFO
        )
        return AnalyzerResult(findings=[finding])

The rules:

  • supports() runs in the main process, so it must be cheap. Look at artifact.detected_type, never at the file contents.
  • analyze() runs in a sandboxed worker. Read the file only with artifact.read(limit). Never write it, run it, render it or open it with another program, and never use the network. The strong sandbox backends block all of these anyway.
  • Catch your own parsing errors and return a finding that says the file couldn't be parsed. An exception that escapes becomes a pipeline.analyzer_error finding with severity high.
  • Give every finding a stable, namespaced rule_id. Use your own prefix, not one of the built-in families.
  • Keep evidence short and escaped. filevet truncates it at 256 characters.
  • Report what you saw. Leave the verdict to the policy.
  • Extracted content (an attachment, an archive entry) goes in AnalyzerResult.children as ExtractedFile(name=..., data=...). The pipeline scans each child with every analyzer, within the recursion limits.
  • Keep the analyzer's state in plain attributes that serialize to JSON. The nsjail and gvisor backends rebuild the analyzer in a fresh process from its class and attributes.

docs.title: Registering it
docs.text:
[project.entry-points."filevet.analyzers"]
"example.seen_text" = "filevet_example_plugin:SeenText"

Install the package next to filevet and check that it shows up:

filevet analyzers

The filevet test suite installs a package like this one from tests/plugin/ to test discovery.

docs.title: Testing it
docs.text:
• A unit test per rule, with inputs that must trigger it and inputs that must not.
  • A test that malformed input produces a finding and not an exception.
  • Build hostile test files with code at test time. Never commit malware, executables or real personal or financial data.

The Analyzer protocol is part of the stable 1.x contract, so a plugin written against 1.0 keeps working until 2.0.

docs.title: Policies
docs.text: Analyzers report what they saw. A policy turns those findings into a verdict: block, review, pass_with_findings or pass. Changing how strict filevet is means changing the policy, never an analyzer.

docs.title: Built-in policies
docs.text:
Name For default high and critical block, medium needs review, anything lower passes with findings. ISO 20022 schema errors are data quality, so they're allowed strict Bank-grade intake. Any active content (malware.*) or parser attack (parser.*) blocks whatever its severity, two or more integrity signals block, and every low or medium finding goes to review ai-ingestion Files that an LLM will read. Hidden text, metadata payloads and Unicode smuggling block, and any prompt injection match goes to review 
filevet scan invoice.pdf --policy strict
filevet scan invoice.pdf --policy ./our-policy.yaml

Library users pass policy=Policy.load("strict"). The API uses FILEVET_POLICY.

docs.title: Format
docs.text:
The format is versioned. Its JSON schema is in schema/policy.schema.json, and filevet schema policy prints it.

policy_version: 1
name: default
rules:
  - match: { severity: critical }
    action: block
  - match: { rule_id: "malware.*", severity: [high] }
    action: block
  - match: { rule_id: "integrity.*" }
    action: review
    when: { min_count: 2 }          # only when several signals combine
  - match: { rule_id: "format.iso20022_schema" }
    action: allow                    # data quality, not security
overrides:
  - match: { rule_id: "malware.pdf_active_content", evidence_contains: "/URI" }
    severity: low
default_action: pass_with_findings
  • match takes rule_id (a glob or a list of globs), severity (one or a list) and evidence_contains. Every key given must match.
  • overrides run first and change a finding's severity in the report. The first matching override wins.
  • Each finding gets the action of the first rule it matches. A rule with when.min_count only counts when at least that many findings match it. Otherwise filevet moves on to the next rule.
  • A finding that matches no rule gets default_action.
  • The verdict is the strictest action across all findings. allow counts as pass. A file with no findings passes.

The report says which rule set the verdict:

"decision": {
  "policy": "default",
  "verdict": "review",
  "rule": 2,
  "rule_ids": ["integrity.iban_not_allowlisted"],
  "reason": "rule 2 of policy default sets review for integrity.iban_not_allowlisted"
}

rule is the index in rules, or null when default_action decided.

docs.title: Testing a policy
docs.text:
make corpus                                    # writes the synthetic corpus to tmp-samples/corpus
filevet policy test strict --corpus tmp-samples/corpus

policy test scans every file in the directory once and shows its verdict under default and under the policy you give, with the rule that decided. Use it on your own sample files before rolling a policy out.

docs.title: Suppressions
docs.text:
A suppression silences one rule for one file, identified by its SHA-256. Every suppression needs a reason and an expiry date.

suppressions:
  - rule_id: parser.csv_formula_injection
    sha256: 3f5a…   # the full 64-character hash of the file
    reason: Supplier export with HYPERLINK formulas, checked by the AP team (ticket FIN-123)
    expires: 2027-03-31

filevet scan export.csv --suppressions suppressions.yaml

Suppressed findings move to the report's suppressed list and don't count towards the verdict. An expired suppression is ignored and adds a warning to the report and to stderr.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text: filevet runs on your own infrastructure and makes no network calls of its own, so files and reports stay with you. The exceptions are the ones you turn on: webhooks send a report to a host you list, and an LLM verifier you install can see findings. Reports can still hold personal data, and the GDPR covers that data if it applies to you. This page lists what a report can contain, so you can decide where to store reports and for how long.

docs.title: What a report contains
docs.text:
• File metadata: the file name, size, SHA-256 and MD5 of the input and of every extracted child. File names often carry names or account numbers (statement_anna_beispiel_2026-01.pdf).
  • Evidence: each finding quotes at most 256 characters of what it saw. For integrity rules that can be a line of text from a statement or invoice, an amount, a date, a person or company name, or a PDF producer string.
  • Locations: page numbers, sheet and cell references, XPaths and byte offsets. On their own these hold no personal data.

docs.title: Masking
docs.text:
IBANs in the evidence are masked by default. The first four and the last four characters stay, and the rest becomes *, so ES9121000418450200051332 shows as ES91 **** **** **** **** 1332. That's enough to match it against your records without storing the full account number. Amounts, dates and names aren't masked, because the reviewer needs them to judge the finding.

filevet scan --no-mask turns masking off. Use it only where the full report is as well protected as the original file.

docs.title: The context file
docs.text: The --context file holds the IBANs of your suppliers, issuer names and certificates. filevet reads it into memory and passes it to the analyzers. It's never logged and never copied into the report. A finding from it says which rule fired and quotes the IBAN from the document, never the one on record.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text: Logs hold SHA-256 hashes, analyzer names, rule IDs, statuses and timings. They never contain file contents, evidence or the context file.

docs.title: The REST API
docs.text: Small uploads are scanned in memory and a private temp directory, and nothing is kept once the response is sent. Large uploads wait in Redis, encrypted, until a worker takes them, and are deleted as it does. Results are kept for FILEVET_RETENTION_S seconds (one hour by default) and then expire. Webhook bodies hold the full report, including evidence.

docs.title: LLM verifiers
docs.text: --llm-verify passes each ai.* finding, with its evidence of at most 256 characters, to the verifier you name. What the verifier does with it, including sending it to a model provider, is up to that plugin. No verifier ships with filevet.

docs.title: What to consider
docs.text:
• Store reports with the same access control and retention as the documents they describe.
  • If you forward reports to a SIEM or ticketing system, keep masking on.
  • A data subject access request may cover reports as well as the original documents.

docs.title: Sanitizing files
docs.text:
filevet sanitize writes a copy of a file with its active content taken out, and prints a report of everything it removed. Use it when a file has to be passed on after the scan. The report is printed even when nothing was removed.

$ filevet sanitize invoice.pdf --output invoice.clean.pdf
{
  "input": "invoice.pdf",
  "output": "invoice.clean.pdf",
  "removed": [
    {"rule_id": "sanitize.javascript", "title": "Removed 1 javascript item(s)", "description": "/JS entries"},
    {"rule_id": "sanitize.annotation", "title": "Removed 2 annotation item(s)", "description": "page 1"}
  ]
}

From Python:

from filevet import sanitize

clean, removed = sanitize("invoice.pdf")

removed is a list of Finding objects with sanitize.* rule IDs and severity info.

The parsing happens inside the configured sandbox, like any analyzer run. If the file can't be parsed, or its type isn't supported, nothing is written and the command exits with code 3.

docs.title: What each type loses
docs.text:
Type Removed Kept PDF Open actions, every /A and /AA action (links, launch, submit-form, JavaScript), JavaScript name trees, embedded files, forms (field values are flattened into the page first) and all annotations Page content, text, images and fonts CSV Nothing is deleted. A cell a spreadsheet would run as a formula gets a leading ', as OWASP recommends. Negative and signed numbers such as -12.50 are left alone Every row and cell, and the delimiter XLSX and XLSM VBA projects and their signatures, XLM macro sheets, external links, the relationships and content types that point at them, and Auto_Open-style defined names. The workbook's content type becomes a plain .xlsx workbook Sheets, cell values, formulas, styles

Rename a sanitized .xlsm to .xlsx, because it no longer has macros.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The output isn't scanned automatically. Run filevet scan on it if it will be trusted further down the line.
  • PDF links stop working, because all annotations are removed rather than sorted into safe and unsafe ones.
  • XLSX formulas are kept. Only CSV cells get the ' prefix.
  • DOCX, PPTX, OLE files (.xls, .doc) and archives aren't supported yet.
  • There's no rasterize-and-OCR mode. It would turn each page into an image and rebuild the text from it, the way Dangerzone does, but that means rendering the hostile file and needs a renderer and an OCR engine. It's a possible future addition and would need its own ADR.

docs.title: Security model
docs.text: filevet parses hostile files on purpose, so its own parsers are the most exposed code it has. Every analyzer run happens inside a sandbox, and the sandbox decides what a compromised parser can still reach. This page covers what each backend guarantees and where each one stops. The reasons behind the design are in ADR 13, and the wider threats are in the threat model.

docs.title: Choosing a backend
docs.text:
Set FILEVET_SANDBOX for the CLI, the API and the workers, or pass sandbox= to scan(), extract_text() and sanitize().

Value Needs Use it for subprocess (default) Linux or macOS Development, CI, and pods that already run under the gVisor RuntimeClass nsjail nsjail on PATH, x86-64, unprivileged user namespaces allowed Production hosts and VMs gvisor runsc on PATH Production hosts with gVisor installed

An unknown value, or a jailed backend whose binary is missing, stops the scan with a usage error instead of falling back to something weaker.

On Ubuntu 24.04 and later, AppArmor blocks unprivileged user namespaces by default. Both nsjail and rootless runsc need them: either allow them with sysctl kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=0 or give the binary its own AppArmor profile.

docs.title: What every backend does
docs.text:
• Each analyzer run gets a new process that handles one artifact and is then killed. No state carries over from one file to the next.
  • The run is limited by --timeout (wall clock) and memory_bytes (address space).
  • The result comes back as JSON and is validated against AnalyzerResult. Oversized results are rejected. Nothing is ever unpickled, in either direction.
  • A timeout, crash, exception or invalid result becomes a pipeline.analyzer_error finding with severity high, so a parser can't hide a file by crashing.
  • Only the exception type reaches the report, never its message.

docs.title: What the jailed backends add
docs.text:
nsjail and gvisor start a new interpreter, python -I -m filevet.core.sandbox, for every run. Inside the jail:

Control nsjail gvisor Network New network namespace with no interfaces, not even loopback --network=none Root filesystem Empty and read-only Empty and read-only (OCI root.readonly) Mounted Python runtime and import path (read-only), the sample at /sample (read-only), /dev/null, /dev/urandom, a tmpfs at /work the size of max_input_bytes The same, plus gVisor's own /proc and /dev User uid and gid 65534, mapped to the filevet user outside uid and gid 65534 inside the sandbox Capabilities None None no_new_privs Yes Yes Seccomp Allow-list (SYSCALLS in core/sandbox.py) as a Kafel policy, everything else returns ENOSYS The same allow-list as an OCI profile, loaded with --oci-seccomp, on top of gVisor's own syscall layer Limits rlimits on address space, CPU seconds, file size, open files (64) and processes (16) The same rlimits, plus memory and PID cgroup limits when runsc runs as root Process creation clone only with CLONE_THREAD, so threads work and fork fails The same

So a parser that a crafted file has taken over can read the sample and the Python files, write up to max_input_bytes into /work, and use CPU and memory until a limit stops it. It can't open a network connection, read /etc or the filevet user's home, write anywhere that survives the run, start processes or gain privileges.

docs.title: Escape tests
docs.text:
tests/unit/test_sandbox.py runs five test-only analyzers through each jailed backend: one opens a socket, one reads /etc/passwd, one writes outside the work directory, one forks in a loop and one allocates past the memory limit. Each attempt must come back as test.blocked or as a pipeline.analyzer_error, never as test.escaped. A sixth, harmless analyzer must succeed, so a jail that can't start Python at all can't pass by blocking everything. The sandbox job in ci.yml builds nsjail from a pinned commit, installs a pinned gVisor release and runs these tests on every pull request.

Run them yourself with uv run pytest -m "requires_nsjail or requires_gvisor". They're skipped when the binaries aren't on PATH.

docs.title: Limits and known gaps
docs.text:
• subprocess isn't a security boundary. It contains crashes, hangs and memory blowups. A compromised parser can still use the network and read whatever the filevet user can. Use it only for development, or inside a pod that's already isolated (see Kubernetes).
  • The Python runtime is readable inside the jail. That includes every directory on sys.path. Don't install filevet into an environment that also holds secrets.
  • execve is allowed, because the jail has to start Python. Only binaries from the mounted directories can be run, and they run under the same restrictions.
  • x86-64 only for nsjail. The allow-list uses x86-64 syscall names. On arm64, use gvisor or the subprocess backend inside a gVisor pod.
  • Rootless gVisor has no cgroup limits. Without root, runsc runs with --rootless --ignore-cgroups, so memory and PID limits come from rlimits alone.
  • Analyzer state must be JSON. The jailed backends rebuild the analyzer from its class and its attributes. Analyzers that keep open handles or compiled objects on self get a pipeline.analyzer_error saying their state is not JSON.
  • Jails cost start-up time. A jailed run takes 0.3 to 1 s against about 20 ms for a fork, mostly for Python start-up and imports. See capacity planning.
  • supports() runs in the parent. It must look only at the detected type, as the analyzer contract already requires.
  • Native parsers aren't fuzzed with coverage. Fuzzing (see fuzzing) instruments filevet's Python code. Native code in qpdf, YARA and expat only gets black-box inputs.

docs.title: Reporting a sandbox escape
docs.text: A file that gets out of the sandbox is a vulnerability. Report it privately as described in SECURITY.md.

docs.title: API stability
docs.text: From 1.0.0, filevet follows semantic versioning. Everything listed on this page is the public API. A minor or patch release won't break it. Anything not listed here can change in any release.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
• The commands scan, extract, sanitize, policy test, serve, worker, analyzers, schema and version, with the options their --help shows.
  • Exit codes:
Code Meaning 0 pass or pass_with_findings, or the command succeeded 1 review, or --fail-on was reached 2 block 3 Usage error: bad arguments, unreadable or oversized input, invalid policy or context file, unsupported type for sanitize 4 Internal error
  • The JSON printed by filevet sanitize: input, output and removed, each item with rule_id, title and description.

The table output format is for people and can change in any release. Use json, sarif, junit or markdown for machines.

docs.title: Report
docs.text:
The report JSON is described by schema/report.schema.json, which filevet schema report prints. 1.0 freezes it at schema_version: 2, the version the Phase 3 release introduced. Minor releases can add optional fields and new rule IDs. Removing or renaming a field, changing its type or adding a verdict raises schema_version and needs a major release.

Rule IDs are stable. A rule can be retired, and its ID is then never reused for something else. Finding titles, descriptions and evidence are meant for people and can change.

docs.title: Policies and suppressions
docs.text: Policy files with policy_version: 1, as described by schema/policy.schema.json (filevet schema policy) and policies.md, and the suppressions file format. The built-in default, strict and ai-ingestion policies can get new rules in minor releases, so pin a policy file of your own if you need verdicts that never move.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
• filevet.scan, filevet.ascan, filevet.extract_text, filevet.sanitize, filevet.Policy, filevet.Report and filevet.__version__, with the parameters they have in 1.0.
  • filevet.core.limits.Limits, filevet.core.analyzer.Expected and filevet.core.errors.ScanError, which those functions take or raise.
  • filevet.core.sandbox.Sandbox and the backend names subprocess, nsjail and gvisor.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
• The filevet.analyzers entry point group and the Analyzer protocol: name, version, supports(artifact) and analyze(artifact, ctx) -> AnalyzerResult.
  • Artifact, AnalysisContext, AnalyzerResult, ExtractedFile, Finding, Location and Severity.
  • The rule that analyzer state must serialize to JSON (see security model).
  • The filevet.llm_verifiers entry point group and the Verifier protocol.

docs.title: REST API
docs.text: Everything under /v1, as described in openapi.json, plus /healthz, /readyz and the metric names on /metrics. Breaking changes go under /v2, and /v1 keeps working for at least one more major release.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: The FILEVET_* environment variables documented in architecture.md, api.md, security-model.md and kubernetes.md, and the Helm chart's values.

docs.title: Not public
docs.text: Modules, functions and attributes whose names start with _. Any module under filevet.analyzers, filevet.interfaces or filevet.core other than the names listed above. The bundled YARA rules. Log line wording (the field names in JSON log events are public). The test corpus and its generators.

docs.title: Deprecation policy
docs.text:
1. A feature is deprecated in a minor release. The CHANGELOG says so, and so do the docs, together with what to use instead.
  2. Using it prints a warning: on stderr for the CLI, as a DeprecationWarning for Python, and as a deprecated log event with the feature's name for the API and workers.
  3. It's removed in the next major release at the earliest, and never sooner than six months after the deprecation.

Security fixes are the one exception. If keeping a feature would leave users exposed, it can be changed or removed in a minor release, with a security advisory explaining why.

docs.title: Support
docs.text: Which releases get fixes is described in SECURITY.md.

docs.title: Threat model
docs.text: This covers the threats filevet looks for in files and the threats against filevet itself. Every file filevet reads may be hostile, so its own parsers are a target.

docs.title: Assets
docs.text:
• The host running filevet: its filesystem, network access, credentials and other workloads.
  • The scanned files: they often hold personal and financial data, so their contents must not leak through logs, reports or temp files.
  • The integrity of the report: a downstream system trusts the verdict. An attacker who can suppress findings or change the verdict can push a malicious file through.
  • The release supply chain: the PyPI package, the container image and their signatures.

docs.title: Attackers
docs.text:
• The file author is the main attacker. They fully control the bytes of the file, and possibly the file name and declared type. They don't control filevet's configuration or the host. They may know exactly which version of filevet is running and craft files to target it.
  • A supply chain attacker tries to get malicious code into filevet's dependencies, build or release.
  • A malicious contributor submits a PR that weakens a check or adds a backdoor.

docs.title: Trust boundaries
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Untrusted
        F[Uploaded file]
    end
    subgraph Pipeline["filevet pipeline (trusted)"]
        I[Ingest and identify]
        A[Aggregate and policy]
    end
    subgraph Sandbox["Analyzer workers (handle hostile data)"]
        P[Parsers and analyzers]
    end
    F --> I --> P -- findings --> A --> R[Report]
  1. File → pipeline. Everything about the file is untrusted, including its name, size, declared type and every byte.
  2. Pipeline → analyzer workers. Parsers are the most exposed code, so they run in isolated workers with time and memory limits. We assume a parser can be compromised by a crafted file.
  3. Workers → aggregation. Findings coming back from a worker are data. They're validated against the Finding model, and their evidence is truncated and escaped before it reaches the report.

docs.title: What filevet must defend against
docs.text: Threat Mitigation Parser exploits (memory corruption in native libraries, logic bugs) Each analyzer in its own process, one task per worker; the nsjail and gvisor backends add namespaces, a seccomp allow-list, a read-only root and dropped privileges, checked by escape tests in CI (security model); nightly coverage-guided fuzzing (fuzzing) Denial of service: zip bombs, entity expansion, huge or deeply nested structures Input size limit, per-analyzer timeout and memory cap, recursion depth, child count and expanded-size limits checked while streaming XXE and network access from parsers defusedxml or lxml with entities and network off; no network in the container; no network interfaces in the nsjail and gvisor sandboxes; a NetworkPolicy that denies worker egress in Kubernetes Path traversal and symlinks during extraction Entries are checked before extraction, symlinks are rejected, children are written only inside the private temp directory Execution of embedded content filevet never runs, renders or opens a file with an external program Data leaking through logs or reports Logs hold hashes, rule IDs and timings only; evidence is truncated and escaped (see architecture) Injection into whatever reads the report (terminal escapes, HTML, CSV formulas) Evidence is escaped; the table view strips control characters Evasion: making an analyzer crash or time out to hide findings A crash or timeout becomes a high severity finding, never a silent pass Leftover files on disk Temp files are deleted after every scan, including on error Supply chain compromise Locked dependencies, license and vulnerability checks in CI, signed releases with SBOMs, trusted publishing without stored tokens Malicious PRs Code owner review on every change, required CI checks, no real malware in the repository Hidden instructions for AI pipelines (invisible text, metadata, Unicode smuggling) ai.* rules on hidden and metadata text, filevet extract --visible-only for ingestion, the ai-ingestion policy Pushing a file through by suppressing its findings Suppressions name one rule and one file hash, need a reason and expire. Expired ones are ignored with a warning, and suppressed findings stay in the report Abuse of the REST API: unauthenticated use, floods, oversized or slow uploads API keys stored as hashes, per-key rate limit, body size counted while streaming, a timeout on every request, at most one synchronous scan per CPU Uploads exposed at rest while queued Encrypted with a key the API and workers share, deleted when a worker takes them, expired after the retention time; Redis runs without persistence in the Compose file Server-side request forgery through webhooks Callbacks only to https URLs on configured hosts, only when a signing secret is set, and without following redirects A pull request steering the GitHub Action through file names or symlinks Paths are passed after --, symlinks are skipped by the Action and refused by filevet scan Active content surviving filevet sanitize Sanitizing parses the file inside the sandbox, removes whole classes of content (all actions and annotations, not a list of bad ones), fails closed when it can't parse the file, and always reports what it removed (sanitize) Injection into SARIF, JUnit or Markdown consumers Text is JSON-encoded, XML-escaped with control characters removed, or Markdown- and HTML-escaped

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text:
• An attacker who already controls the host or filevet's configuration.
  • Malware that filevet has no rule for. A missed detection is a bug to fix, but filevet never claims to catch everything.
  • What happens to the file after filevet hands back its report.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: filevet is a security tool that outside contributors will review and extend. They need to know why it's built the way it is, not only how.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: We record significant decisions as Architecture Decision Records in docs/adr/, in the short format from Michael Nygard's Documenting Architecture Decisions: context, decision, consequences. Files are numbered in order. An accepted ADR isn't edited; when a decision changes, a new ADR supersedes it.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Decisions are reviewed in PRs like code. Adding a runtime dependency or changing a core design choice means writing or updating an ADR.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: filevet's users are fintechs and finance teams, whose legal departments often restrict which open-source licenses they accept. Copyleft licenses such as the GPL and AGPL are frequently blocked for internal and SaaS use. A security tool also benefits from a clear patent grant, so users and contributors know they won't be sued over patents in the code.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: filevet is licensed under Apache-2.0, with a NOTICE file holding the copyright line. Runtime dependencies must use licenses compatible with Apache-2.0. CI enforces this with an allow-list.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Companies can use filevet and build on it without legal friction, including in closed products. Contributions come with an explicit patent license. Some dependencies are off-limits: GPL-only libraries can't be bundled. ClamAV is GPL, so it runs as a separate service (see ADR 5) and is never linked.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Most of the work is parsing file formats and looking for known patterns. The best open-source libraries for that are in Python: pikepdf and pdfminer.six for PDF, oletools for Office macros, defusedxml and lxml for XML, yara-python for YARA. Security and data teams, the people likely to contribute analyzers, already know Python. filevet parses hostile input, so memory safety is a real concern.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: filevet is written in Python and supports 3.11 and newer. We use type hints everywhere and run mypy in strict mode on the core. uv manages dependencies and the lock file.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: We get mature parsing libraries and a low barrier for contributors. Python is slower than compiled languages, which is acceptable at our target of a 20 MB PDF in under 10 seconds. Several of these libraries wrap native code that can have memory-safety bugs, so we don't rely on the language for safety: parsers run in isolated workers (see the architecture) and get fuzzed in Phase 4.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted
